sm: Host Jeremy Boreing opens a conversation about the split on the American right after what he calls the midterm bloodbath. People blame the war, tariffs, immigration raids or online pessimism, while a newer wing says the problem is the American system itself. He introduces Christian Heinz, Joel Berry and their mutual friend Nick Fratus, and says it is an open conversation rather than a formal debate. Christian says he and Joel disagree on a lot, but both are closer to each other than to the left, so the right must hang together. A guest describes himself as a normal Baptist-raised conservative who came back from Iraq determined to protect America, and says the differences surfaced once the right won and had to decide what it wanted to build.

A guest says he first noticed the divide over a racial tinge in the immigration debate and over the Christ is King chant, which he says Nick Fuentes started to push Jews out of the movement. He says he began reading Schmitt, Evola and Guenon after seeing a tweet from Christian joking about a plan to red-pill normies with them. He reads a passage from Evola about liberating the world from God and calls it foreign to American conservatism. Christian jokes that his election-data step did not go to plan, since he predicted Republican losses in the midterms and was too optimistic. He recommends Evola's short work Orientations, which he says warns against fascism and progressivism, and says Evola should not be judged only by his most anti-Christian phase.

Christian says he does not accept Evola's pagan imperialism as a Christian, but finds value in parts of Orientations, and the others reply that critiques of progressivism are nothing new. Jeremy sets a ground rule to talk about the divide in plain human terms rather than through obscure philosophers, noting that many people pick sides tribally without knowing the terms. Another guest says he and Christian talk for an hour after every podcast, and that online shorthand, like the phrase identity politics, causes people to talk past each other. He argues these thinkers have diagnosed real problems modern conservatism has not faced, though he thinks most of their solutions are garbage.

One speaker says he loves the Constitution and the founding philosophy, and he raises a worry that the Constitution permits its own legal destruction. He imagines Democrats winning a trifecta, stacking the Supreme Court and reinterpreting the document through legal means, and says vote harder is not enough for him. Jeremy asks Christian whether he accepts the founding or sees America as a product of the Enlightenment. Christian says the neo-reactionary view treats America as the root of liberal modernity, but he disagrees, because the American Revolution sought to reclaim the rights of Englishmen. He sees a direct line from the French Revolution to progressivism, but not from the American one.

Christian describes the Greek historian Polybius and the cycle of governments from monarchy to aristocracy to democracy to mob rule and back, and says Rome's mixed constitution broke the cycle. He says the American founding drew on that tradition, so he can take pride in it. Jeremy asks both sides what they actually want, listing the loss of family, virtue and community, and mass immigration eroding a shared national culture. Joel says the only hope is Christian revival. He argues against the idea that the right mix of people automatically produces good law, saying it ignores human depravity, and points to the Israelites worshipping the golden calf as proof that law comes from above.

Joel continues with the Pilgrims, who he says tried a socialist commune and nearly starved until William Bradford introduced private property. Another speaker asks whether people wrongly assume you can import anyone and they will become Americans. Jeremy says no one really believes that, but that assimilation fails when tens of millions arrive quickly while being taught that their own culture is superior and the melting pot is racist. He criticizes parts of the right for inventing a unified white European identity, arguing that Europeans spent centuries killing each other and that immigration worked when the numbers, origins and incentives were right. He adds that even people from Somalia could assimilate in small numbers over time.

The four agree that nobody at the table thinks the American system is uniquely white. One says progressivism is a white value and that white thinkers like Marx, Marcuse and Foucault created the ideas wrecking the country. Another says people who make cultural distinctions are not automatically making racial ones, and calls Nick Fuentes a motte-and-bailey arguer he would not talk to. They agree social media algorithms reward distorted framings, so face-to-face talk helps. Pressed on what restores what has been lost, Joel says it is slow generational work of rekindling faith and raising Christian children. He says the right is becoming post-Christian, putting faith in power and tactics, when the founding was blessed because it was Christian.

Christian speaks for younger men on the right. He says the first time he heard white man used as an insult was in college, and that younger men have grown up with their arguments dismissed over race and sex. They concluded that debate and discourse are dead, and that conservatives only told them to vote harder, which pushed them toward elite theory and a friend-enemy view of politics. He says younger men are scared about the future and are drifting toward racial thinking, which he does not endorse. Jeremy agrees, saying if you treat a generation of boys as racists they will become racists, as a husband treated as a cheat eventually becomes one. Another speaker warns against adopting left-style critical theory for right-wing ends.

Christian says institutions that betrayed people, such as in COVID, led some young men to believe the opposite of whatever institutions say, even flirting with Nazi ideas. Another speaker says the new right at least coddles these men and black-pills them about needing a strongman, and those who push back get called neocons. Christian says there is also a right hand of progressivism, and that he sees the others as fellow travelers. One guest says he once interviewed figures from Doug Wilson to Orin McIntyre to James Lindsay and could live in any of their Americas, since the real difference is the route. Christian says he works in Virginia politics, where Republicans keep losing, and that he feels the car is already going off the cliff.

Jeremy asks what mechanism a new-right strongman could use, citing a figure who says democracy is not needed to get their way. He notes that only about sixty percent of Americans are Christian, around fifty-seven percent are white, and the military is not majority white, so no army or majority exists for it. He doubts monarchy delivers, noting the Bible and Rome had few good kings. Christian answers that we live in a fallen world and every step should make the next one easier. He gives Donald Trump credit for the first net decrease in immigration in over fifty years, calling it good but not enough, and blames Congress for not doing more.

Christian says Congress passed little beyond the one big beautiful bill, and could have stripped lower courts of jurisdiction over deportation cases, using the Kilmar Abrego Garcia case as an example. The group discusses Godel's supposed loophole in the Constitution and whether the answer to a weak Congress is a Hamilton-style lifetime president. Christian says he does not think the country is at a Weimar moment yet, and admits that in 2024 he expected Republicans to lose, so Trump's win felt like a miracle. Jeremy presses on how the rebels of the American Revolution lacked a majority, and a guest replies that they were expelling a foreign army, not fighting countrymen, adding that some Americans are countrymen only legally.

One guest says this is no longer a debate between countrymen but between opposed worldviews, and that one side will win. He recalls his time in the Virginia legislature, where Republicans funded the colleges and institutions he opposed, and says the left dominates media, academia and the bureaucracy. Another replies that weakness within an institution is not an argument against the institution, and that the left has entropy on its side. Joel says people want a magic bullet like a king, as with Bukele, but that good kings are rare in the Bible and in Europe, and that even David murdered a man. He cites the prophet Samuel's warning and says rolling the dice on a prince risks centuries of tyranny.

A guest says he still wants to strip lower courts of oversight and fix the system's checks and balances, not install a Caesar. Others say the right talks about Franco Friday and inevitability, but nothing is inevitable. The guest says some Democrats are not his countrymen, since they use constitutional protections to destroy the constitution. He predicts Democrats will win a trifecta in 2028, end the filibuster and stack the Supreme Court, and proposes the Kentucky and Virginia resolutions, with states such as Tennessee refusing to enforce rulings, as nullification. Asked whether he would fight on a Franco-style side, he says he would have sided with Franco against the communists, and would use force against a stacked court.

Jeremy says the doom has not happened yet and many on the right act as if it has. Speakers criticize accelerationism and those who told Republicans to vote Democrat, and note Texas just went blue. Jeremy argues that human agency means voters change, that Puerto Rican statehood could be reversed, and that illiberalism, not liberalism, freezes people in place. He says conservative wins are real, including the end of Roe versus Wade and net negative immigration. He argues the right understates evils such as abortion, the transgender agenda, telling Gen Z they are Nazis and no-fault divorce, which he says harmed them more than progressive teaching. He closes by saying evil will only end when Christ returns, so conservatives should take the wins.

Jeremy says Trump never marshaled Congress and that Paul Ryan gave him his main legislative wins. He argues young people have reason for hope, noting that millennials once told they would never build wealth are now the richest cohort, and that entrepreneurship among people in their twenties is at an all-time high. He says there are more factory jobs than workers and that tariffs would mostly bring immigrants and robots. He admits real affordability pressures on Gen Z and that young women and men are being set against each other, but says it is a left-wing view that circumstances decide your fate. Boomers also faced Vietnam, and each generation had its own hardships.

Jeremy says great things like catching rockets come from a system that rewards great men, and heritage Americans cannot throw out what their fathers fought for. He argues the founders sought a place where a man is free, rather than an ethno-state, and that revolutionary impulses have rarely produced anything better than what we have. Someone asks whether power reveals or corrupts and jokes that Jeremy should hold power. Jeremy says the right must not exclude people over foreign policy while including those who back left-wing economics, urge votes for Democrats or call for killing opponents. He criticizes figures who say neocons should be shut out, and replies that Trump alone started the Iran war.

Jeremy says the war with Iran was Trump's executive decision with no national debate, so blaming neocons is wrong. Speakers agree that anyone telling people to vote Democrat is on the enemy side. One defends Orin McIntyre as wanting the Constitution restored, not overthrown, and notes Fuentes blocks him. Jeremy says the new right applies a no enemies to the right rule, and says he is not black-pilled, telling students that godly families can win within one generation because the left needs mass immigration and institutions. A guest recalls telling a colleague offstage that he had been behind a fifty-caliber gun at twenty-five. Another says people who show up late should not dictate what the movement must be.

Christian says he has been a loyal Republican since before he could vote, door-knocking at seventeen. He describes working with Cliff Maloney on a Pennsylvania early-vote effort at the request of Charlie Kirk, and calling Pennsylvania for Trump on election night before the networks. He is hurt that James Lindsay, who once voted for Obama, calls him woke right. Another guest says he is hurt when dissident right figures call him a leftist, but his real objection is philosophical. He says Orin McIntyre's idea that the Constitution comes from a people leads toward racial pride, and that claiming whiteness is why America is free is a reactionary lie feeding wounded pride. He says as long as he is breathing his answer is not today.

A guest says the total-state idea tells people to accept they live under tyranny and pick their own tyrant, and he rejects it. Another says Orin did not want a Red Caesar, and that these figures are better in private than online. Joel describes a debate in which Dave Green said a Christian government would see the Constitution as heretical and favor a two-tier justice system by race. Christian defends Green, saying he was making a different point about outcomes under colorblind law. They argue about whether everyone is imposing a metaphysics, with Joel saying there is an American one and that the new right would be the ones changing it.

Joel says Americans are trying to conserve the metaphysics handed down from the founding, rooted in the Declaration, Constitution and Christianity, and are not forcing something new. Christian replies that the actual order has changed through the New Deal, Wilson, Lincoln and civil rights. He describes a friend named Kaiser who quoted Jefferson without attribution, and reads Jefferson's letter saying written law can yield to the needs of national survival. Joel says the founders disagreed, so values come from the founding documents and Christianity. A guest says he respects both men and does not think they are enemies, only that they disagree about the threat and the response.

One guest says he is watching the Democratic party gather power, and he cites Virginia officials building permanent bureaucracies. He asks who will stand beside him if a stacked court voids the right to bear arms and a future president orders troops to confiscate weapons. He says he is trying to prevent a king, not create one. Jeremy says his dividing line excludes racists and anti-Semites, and that evil done in his name bothers him more than evil by opponents. A guest says that if he were dictator he would repeal the progressive amendments, though he hesitates over women's suffrage. Jeremy says the country remains better than any alternative, and that American Christianity outlasted the established churches of Europe.

Jeremy says American creedalism is not responsible for progressivism, and notes that England kept its king and is worse off. He argues for conserving the best of the inheritance and fixing what does not work. Christian says the right needs a new fusionism for the twenty-first century like Reagan's coalition of hawks, social conservatives and free marketeers, and that the friend-enemy idea does not apply to individuals within a coalition. He would oppose populist economic leftism internally but not at the cost of losing to people he accuses of mutilating children. He will not caucus with race essentialists, anti-Semites or those who want a Christian prince. Another says the new right gives the left a foil and helped cause the midterm losses.

A guest says you cannot out-left the left or be a better tyrant than leftists. As the conversation wraps, another says he would be the last to pull the trigger, that some Christians romanticize persecution, and that he does not want hard times or a war with millions of countrymen dead. He says it is not that nothing is worth fighting for, but no one should fantasize about it. If the fight is for what is good he will stand alongside others, and if both sides are bad he will start an underground church. He says his son joined the infantry after prayer, that preparedness is meant to deter conflict, and that he hopes a generation will overcome evil with good. The four thank each other and end the evening.
